cold.headline: BalloutDaDon Arrested for Attempted Murder at Trippie Redd's Home
cold.author: C. Vernon Coleman II
cold.body:
Police execute a search warrant on Trippie Redd 's South Florida home and arrest rapper BalloutDaDon for attempted murder.
On Tuesday (Oct. 6), the Davie Police Department searched Trippie's property in Southwest Ranches, Fla., a DPD spokesperson confirmed to XXL on Wednesday (Oct. 7). The search was done in conjunction with the Miami Police Department. MPD confirmed to XXL that Balllout, born Braveone Jones, 25, was the target of the search and he has been taken into custody.
"Jones faces two counts of attempted murder in connection with the Sept. 15, 2026 shooting at Dukunoo Jamaican Kitchen," an MPD spokesperson tells XXL . "The investigation remains ongoing."
An 18-year-old man and a 23-year-old man were shot outside Dukunoo Jamaican Kitchen in the Wynwood section of Miami on Sept. 15, according to NBC 6 South Florida . Both victims were taken to Jackson Memorial Hospital's Ryder Trauma Center in serious but stable condition. At the time of the shooting, police didn't have any information on the shooter or what prompted the violent incident.
BalloutDaDon, a Trippie Redd affiliate who is signed to the independent label HAB ENT, has released music with Luhh Dyl, 1900Rugrat and others. He's released two projects in 2026: Yopstar and Yopstar Lyfestyle 2 .
Trippie Redd is on the heels of releasing his first album in three years, NDA, and the follow-up #NDA .

cold.headline: Phono V streaming rate proposals filed with US Copyright Royalty Board, as DIMA points to 30% growth in publishing revenues since 2022
cold.kicker: The proceeding will set the mechanical rates on-demand streaming services pay US songwriters and publishers from 2028 through 2032. Source
cold.author: Mandy Dalugdug
cold.body:
Parties to Phonorecords V have submitted their written testimony and rate proposals to the US Copyright Royalty Board (CRB).
This part of the proceeding will set the mechanical royalty rates that on-demand streaming services pay songwriters and publishers in the US between 2028 and 2032 .
The filings were made on Monday (October 5), the deadline the CRB had set for participants that had not reached a settlement.
The Digital Media Association (DIMA), the trade body representing music streaming services in the US, said in a statement on Tuesday (October 6) that it looked forward to a “timely resolution” of the proceeding. Its members include Amazon , Apple Music , Feed.fm , Pandora , Qobuz , Spotify , Tidal , and YouTube .
The trade body pointed to data from the National Music Publishers’ Association (NMPA) showing that US music publishing revenues have grown by more than 30% , from USD $5.6 billion in 2022 to $7.3 billion in 2025.
Spotify , Apple , Amazon , Google , and Pandora are all participants in the proceeding, according to the CRB’s online docket.
Opposite them are the NMPA and the Nashville Songwriters Association International (NSAI), which participate jointly as the “Copyright Owners.”
The three major record companies, filing jointly as the Joint Record Company Participants, and the American Association of Independent Music ( A2IM ) are also participants.
Other participants include the Songwriters Guild of America (SGA), Word Collections , Eminem publisher Eight Mile Style (listed as Eight Mile Music Companies), the Music Artists Coalition , and Nashville songwriter George Johnson .

cold.headline: ‘You think you’re invincible, and you’re not’: Gretta Ray on sickness, surviving and finding her new sound
cold.kicker: After a life-threatening infection, the Australian singer-songwriter has rebuilt her relationship with music – and her third album ‘sounds nothing like the last’ The illness that almost killed Gretta Ray announced itself
cold.author: Katie Cunningham
cold.body:
After a life-threatening infection, the Australian singer-songwriter has rebuilt her relationship with music – and her third album ‘sounds nothing like the last’
The illness that almost killed Gretta Ray announced itself slowly. First there were chills that had her inexplicably shivering under the doona. Then came gastrointestinal symptoms; next a splitting headache. Fatigue flattened her, keeping her in bed for days. But it was when the singer-songwriter woke up one morning with double vision that she knew something was really wrong. Ray went straight to hospital – and stayed there for six weeks. After a long and agonising slew of tests, she was diagnosed with infective endocarditis, a life-threatening infection of the heart that can cause a strange, gradual march of symptoms.
Ray was put on an antibiotic drip “pretty much 24 hours a day”, which saved her life. But at just 26 years old, her age made her an outlier on the cardiology ward – and forced some big psychological reckonings.
“Being young and being motivated and ambitious, you think you’re invincible, and you’re not,” she says. “The scariest part of it all was not being able to be told that I was going to be OK … That’s going to live with me for ever, and there are still times when I find myself getting anxious and thinking those terrifying thoughts – like, ‘maybe you’ll die’.”
If her words leave a heaviness hanging in the air, Ray doesn’t leave long before puncturing it. “Welcome to my trauma-dumping session!” she laughs.

cold.headline: ‘In the wake of death, Courtney Love was giving it her all’: Hole’s Melissa Auf der Maur on her best photograph
cold.kicker: ‘This is Courtney doing her makeup on the ’95 Lollapalooza tour. I was documenting my generation being hijacked by corporate greed – and destroyed following the sacrificial death of Kurt Cobain’ When I was going through
cold.author: Interview by Zoe Whitfield
cold.body:
‘This is Courtney doing her makeup on the ’95 Lollapalooza tour. I was documenting my generation being hijacked by corporate greed – and destroyed following the sacrificial death of Kurt Cobain’
W hen I was going through the archives for my rock photo book, I came across my first ever self-portrait, at Père Lachaise Cemetery in Paris, in front of Jim Morrison’s grave. I am a 13-year-old on an awkward trip with my cool father. He had no respect or interest in Jim Morrison, and that photo is like every photo I’ve taken from that moment on – I’m trying to take agency over what is happening. Photography was the absolute first thing that gave me a feeling of having my own say. It became a way of creating my own universe, one that I could trust. It was absolutely my first love.
I was sidetracked into music in a beautiful way by these radical women and a countercultural movement, so the subject of my photographs just changed. It was me within this environment, on stage with Hole, backstage with these luminary, wild people, travelling across the world. My photography followed and morphed with me, and my camera documented my generation being hijacked by corporate greed and destroyed in the wake of the sacrificial death of Kurt Cobain. It was a generational call to document the Lollapalooza ’95 tour, where this photo was taken, for us to understand later. It was also when the wild alternative freaks crossed into the mainstream.

cold.author: Iman Amrani
cold.body:
After representing society’s dispossessed, Ponder started a music career in her 40s – then faced miscarriage, anxiety and more. She explains her survival instinct
“You can get everything you dreamed of career-wise, and your life can still crumble, and that is what happened to me,” says US singer-songwriter Danielle Ponder.
Five years ago, and five days before her 40th birthday, Ponder left her job as a public defender – a lawyer for those without the means to pay for one – to pursue music full-time. Ponder’s rich, church-reared voice and resonant music quickly lent themselves to cinematic moments: she wrote and performed the theme song for Apple TV+’s Manhunt and her trip-hop-infused track Roll the Credits has been used by adverts, TV shows and video games. Several comments on the YouTube video come from viewers who searched for it thinking she was Nina Simone. Her debut album, Some of Us Are Brave, came out in 2022 and was warmly received by critics, and she appeared on Seth Meyers’ talkshow. Her gamble had paid off. “But personally,” she says, “it felt like everything around me was falling apart”.
